title: Data Retention
summary: Data retention is the practice of deciding in advance how long each category of data is kept and what happens when that period ends. A retention schedule names the data, the lawful or business reason for holding it, the period, the storage location and the destruction method, because keeping data indefinitely increases both breach impact and legal exposure once it can no longer be justified. Periods are usually set by whichever is longer, a legal or contractual duty or a genuine operational need, then applied automatically through lifecycle rules on object storage, databases and backup rotation. The common mistake is treating archives and backups as exempt: they contain the same personal data, and a deletion that never reaches the backup cycle comes back after the next restore. Deletion has to be evidenced, not assumed, and legal holds must be able to pause it deliberately.

beginner.definition: Data retention means deciding how long you keep each kind of data. It also means deciding what you do with that data at the end. Some records must be kept for legal or business reasons. Everything else should be deleted when there is no longer a good reason to hold it.
beginner.whyItMatters: Data you no longer need is still a risk. If an attacker steals it, the harm is the same as if you used it every day. Old records also make legal requests harder to answer, because you must search more places. Keeping data forever can break privacy duties and surprise you in an audit. Clear time limits make deletion normal instead of a special project.
howItWorks: List each type of data your team holds, such as invoices, tickets or customer files.
Find the legal or business reason for keeping each type of data.
Set a retention period for each one, and write that period down.
Choose where the data lives, and how deletion will happen in that place.
Automate deletion with lifecycle rules, so the work does not depend on memory.
Include backups and archives in the plan, and prove that deletion really happened.
beginner.example: Think of a library that keeps a slip for every book borrowed. The slips help staff find overdue books, so they are useful for a while. After a few years the slips are no longer needed, and keeping them means storing boxes of private reading habits. The librarian agrees a rule: keep each slip for one year, then shred it on the same day each month. If the shredding never reaches the storage room upstairs, the rule is not real. A good retention rule names the shelf, the time and the person who clears it.
takeaways: Write the retention period and the deletion method together.
Backups and archives hold the same data, so include them.
Automate deletion, and keep evidence that it ran.

objectives: Explain what data retention means and why indefinite storage is a risk.
Describe the elements of a retention schedule that make it enforceable.
Identify how legal duties and operational needs set a retention period.
Explain how backups and archives affect deletion commitments.
Describe how evidence of deletion is produced and kept.
